Live: https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/ and https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/run.html#ex=dbt
- Core story facts: FirstRun runs a docs quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, fixes it, and proves the fix with a second clean run. Real wins: dbt guide `jafgen --years 6` broke in jafgen 0.4.6 (2024-04-07), fix proven 9/9 in a fresh container, upstream PRs dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149 and #10150, entireio/cli#2724. B-roll list for the DJI Action 4: each shot with framing, mount/angle (chest mount, desk clamp, low-angle, POV over shoulder, timelapse), lens mode, frame rate (e.g. 4K 60 or 120 for slow-mo), lighting note, duration, and which beat it serves. 6. Three reference demos for inspiration (real, well-known product launch videos, e.g. Linear, Vercel, Arc, Apple) with one line each on what to borrow. Only cite ones you are confident exist.

Report back the absolute file path and a 5-line summary of the story spine.

8	
9	# Runtime Contract
10	
11	> **Purpose:** This file says which rules load, in what order, and which checks run at the end.
12	> It is the only file that answers "what was applied to this draft". Read it first, every time.
13	> Adapted from the runtime contract in [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer).
14	> The architecture is theirs. The rules and the voice are mine.
15	
16	## Always loaded
17	
18	Six files load for every piece of writing, on every channel, in this order.
19	
20	1. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, this file. The load order and the checks.
21	2. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`. The failure patterns a regex cannot see.
22	3. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/write-simply.md`. The plain style, and the test for whether the ideas are right.
23	4. `DIGITAL TWIN/World.md`. The villain, the vision, and what the piece is for.
24	5. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. The bar the insight clears before a word is drafted.
25	6. `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`. How the writing sounds.
26	
27	Files 2 and 3 are a pair. The pattern rules say what to remove, and `write-simply.md` says what to
28	aim for, so a draft that only obeys the first one reads stripped.
29	
30	`World.md` decides what the piece argues and `Voice.md` decides how it sounds, so the two never
31	collide. Name the skill-tree node before you draft a line. A piece that advances no node is an
32	idea, so send it back to `SUBSTACK/0_IDEAS/`.
33	
34	`net-new-value.md` is the guiding principle for all content, on every channel. Write the core
35	insight as one sentence and name its box before you draft. Only box 4 ships: non-obvious to the
36	reader and tactical enough to use today. A piece outside box 4 gets one upgrade, then goes back to
37	the idea bank.
38	
39	`SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` holds the banned words, phrases and punctuation. `DIGITAL TWIN/rules/`
40	holds the prose rules, one file each. The `core` rules load into every session through the generated
41	block in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so you never copy them into another file.
42	
43	The `craft` rules load for every writing job. Run this once per session before the first draft:
44	
45	```bash
46	python SCRIPTS/slop/rules_prompt.py --profile craft
47	```
48	
49	## Loaded on demand
50	
51	One more file loads, chosen by the job. Never load two.
52	
53	| The job | Load this |
54	|---|---|
55	| A Substack article, an essay, a long piece | `DIGITAL TWIN/Long-Form Writing Rules.md` |
56	| A tutorial, a how-to, a README, developer docs | `DIGITAL TWIN/Technical Writing Style Guide.md` |
57	| A LinkedIn post, a Note, a tweet, a caption | nothing extra. The channel skill carries it |
58	
59	`DIGITAL TWIN/AI Writing Policy.md` outranks all of the above and it changes rarely, so read it
60	when you start a writing session and not once per draft.
61	
62	## Then the channel skill
63	
64	The skill carries the shape of the channel and nothing else. It never restates a banned word, a
65	voice rule or a craft rule, because a copy goes stale and then two files disagree.
66	
67	| Channel | Skill |
68	|---|---|
69	| LinkedIn post | `.claude/skills/write-linkedin-posts/SKILL.md` |
70	| X post or thread | `.claude/skills/banger-tweets/SKILL.md` |
71	| Substack Note | `.claude/skills/substack-notes/SKILL.md` |
72	| Substack article | `.claude/skills/substack-writer/SKILL.md` |
73	| Reddit post | none. `SOCIALS/Reddit/README.md` is the channel spec |
74	| Landing page or sales email | `.claude/skills/write-sales-copy/SKILL.md` |
75	| A stuck idea with no shape yet | `.claude/skills/write-outline/SKILL.md` |
76	| An existing draft that reads like AI | `.claude/skills/deslop-audit/SKILL.md` |
77	
78	## Precedence, higher wins
79	
80	Four layers can disagree. Resolve upward.
81	
82	1. The banned lists in `slop_rules.py` and the patterns in `core/pattern-rules.md`.
83	2. The channel skill.
84	3. `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`.
85	4. A sample Atharva pastes in the current session.
86	
87	A sample beats the profile. The profile beats the skill. Two rules never override anything above
88	them. The fabrication rule below, and the five principles in `AI Writing Policy.md`.
89	
90	## The fabrication rule
91	
92	Add no fact that Atharva did not supply. That covers a name, a number, a date, a statistic, a
93	quote, a source, an event and a client. This rule bites hardest on a rewrite, because the fix for
94	a vague sentence looks like a specific sentence, and the specifics are not yours to invent.
95	
96	You have three legal moves when a sentence needs a real detail.
97	
98	1. Ask him for it.
99	2. Mark the gap in visible brackets, such as `[the real number]`. Brackets cannot ship by accident.
100	3. Drop the claim to the level the evidence supports, or cut it.
101	
102	An invented specific that reads well is a worse defect than the vague sentence it replaced. A
103	reader cannot catch it.
104	
105	## The two-pass loop
106	
107	Never hand over a first draft.
108	
109	**Pass 1.** Write it. Do not judge while you write.
110	
111	**Pass 2.** Read it cold and answer five questions for yourself, in writing. Do not print the
112	answers unless he asks.
113	
114	1. If a reader called this AI, which exact sentence would they point at?
115	2. Does the draft carry a fact, a name, a number or a source that he did not give me?
116	3. Which sentence is the weakest, and does the piece rest on it?
117	4. Which sentence reads worst, and is the idea under it wrong rather than the wording?
118	5. Is the core insight still box 4 in `core/net-new-value.md`, or did the draft sand it down to box 2?
119	
120	**Pass 3.** Fix what the answers found. Then run the checks.
121	
122	## Announce the load order
123	
124	Render this panel above every draft. Do not type it by hand.
125	
126	```bash
127	python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill <channel skill> --file "<path>"     --node "<the skill-tree node this piece advances>"     --topic "<the idea, for the pillar check>"     --season "<NN beat N, or none>" --format "<number and name, or n/a>"     --insight "<the box 4 insight, one sentence>"
128	```
129	
130	`--glob "<pattern>"` replaces `--file` for a batch, and reports the worst result
131	across the set. `--plain` drops to ASCII. `--technical` swaps the on-demand file
132	for the Technical Writing Style Guide. The script exits 1 when any measured check
133	failed, so a caller can gate on it.
134	
135	```
136	╭─ LOAD ORDER ─────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
137	│ ✓ 1  core/runtime-contract              always               │
138	│ ✓ 2  core/pattern-rules                 always               │
139	│ ✓ 3  core/write-simply                  always               │
140	│ ✓ 4  World.md                           always               │
141	│ ✓ 5  core/net-new-value                 always               │
142	│ ✓ 6  Voice.md                           always               │
143	│ ✓ 7  Long-Form Writing Rules.md         on demand            │
144	│ ✓ 8  skill:substack-writer              channel              │
145	├─ WORLD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
146	│ villain  rented work                                         │
147	│ node     builds a gate that refuses bad work                 │
148	│ season   01 beat 3      format  05 Contrarian Take           │
149	│ insight  a hook that returns decision: block stops the save  │
150	├─ CHECKS, measured ───────────────────────────────────────────┤
151	│ ✓ pillar      ON (AI)                                        │
152	│ ✓ slop        CRIT 0                                         │
153	│ ✓ clarity     CRIT 0                                         │
154	│ ✓ craft       0                                              │
155	│ ✓ seo         CRIT 0                                         │
156	╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
157	```
158	
159	The two halves carry different weight, and the difference is the point.
160	
161	**The top half is declared.** You state the node, the season and the box 4 insight. The chain itself
162	comes from the channel table inside the script, so it cannot drift from this file.
163	
164	**The bottom half is measured.** The script runs each scorer and prints what it
165	returned. A tick means a check ran and passed. A cross means it ran and failed. A
166	dot means the scorer could not run, which never reads as a pass.
167	
168	That split is why the panel replaced the four hand-typed lines it used to be. A
169	typed line could claim `slop CRIT 0` for a check nobody ran, which is the blind
170	spot this contract exists to close. A rendered line cannot.
171	
172	A missing panel means the chain was skipped.
173	
174	## The checks, in this order
175	
176	Run them in order. A later check on a draft that fails an earlier one wastes both your time and his.
177	
178	| Order | Command | Bar |
179	|---|---|---|
180	| 0 | Name the box in `core/net-new-value.md` for the one-sentence insight | Box 4. Every channel |
181	| 0b | The opening gate in `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md` | The top-ranked of 5 openings ships, and no hook is a question. LinkedIn, X, Notes |
182	| 1 | `python SCRIPTS/pillars/pillars.py --text "<the idea>"` | ON, or an honest BEND |
183	| 2 | `python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py check "<the idea>"` | WRITE. Articles only |
184	| 3 | `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` | CRIT reaches 0 |
185	| 4 | `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"` | CRIT reaches 0. Every channel |
186	| 5 | `python SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py "<file>"` | CRIT reaches 0. LinkedIn only |
187	| 6 | `python SCRIPTS/substack/craft.py "<file>"` | 0. Articles only |
188	| 7 | `python SCRIPTS/seo/score.py "<file>" --write` | 0. Articles only |
189	| 8 | `python SCRIPTS/socials/coverage.py` | no `source_blog` warning. Social files only |
190	| 9 | `python SCRIPTS/review/build.py` | the desk carries it. Every draft is on it, nothing to stamp |
191	
192	Rows 4, 5 and 6 were missing from this table until 2026-09-04. All three existed
193	and two of them already blocked a commit, so the table was the only place that
194	disagreed. A check absent from this file gets skipped by anyone who trusts it,
195	which is the whole reason the file exists. Add a row here in the same commit
196	that adds a scorer.
197	
198	Checks 0, 0b, 1 and 2 run before you draft. Checks 3 to 9 run after. Skip a row only when the row says
199	so, and say in the announcement block which rows you skipped.
200	
201	MED and LOW findings from the scorer are advisory. On short-form, ignore its flow, paragraph and
202	fragment findings, because those rules were written for long-form.

The first post in the file publishes immediately. Every post after it takes the next free slot, three per day, at 10:00, 14:30 and 19:30 IST. The first slot used is the next one still in the future, so a run started at 01:00 fills today and a run started at 20:00 starts tomorrow.

Dry run is the default on every command. Nothing leaves the machine without `--live`.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `plan <file>` | Print the schedule, character counts and image flags. Sends nothing. |
| `send <file> --live` | Publish post 1 now, schedule the rest, append to `_sent.tsv`. |
| `sync-media <file> --live` | Attach images to posts that are **already scheduled**, matched on exact text. |
| `list` | Print the whole Zernio queue with status, time and image flag. |
| `publish <post_id> --live` | Send a scheduled post right now instead of waiting for its slot. |
| `cancel <post_id> --live` | Delete one scheduled post. |
| `schedule <file> --at "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM" [--every N]` | Schedule at a time you pick, stepping N days per post. Publishes nothing now. |
| `respace --pin <id,id,...>` | Re-space the whole queue onto the slot grid, order kept. Pinned ids hold their time. |

`publish` refuses anything that is not currently scheduled, so it cannot double-post something already live. Publishing early leaves its old slot empty and moves nothing else, so the rest of the queue keeps the times it was given.

Add `--platform youtube` to target another account. The default is `twitter`.

## Picking the time yourself, and fixing an overbooked queue

`send` always publishes post 1 immediately and drops the rest into the next free grid slots. That
is wrong for a post that has to land in one specific slot, so `schedule` takes the time from you.

```bash
python SCRIPTS/zernio/post.py schedule "SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_Foo.md" --at "2026-08-30 19:30" --live
```

# FirstRun Business Plan

FirstRun runs a dev tool's quickstart in a clean container every night, finds the first step that breaks, proves the fix with a second clean run, and drafts the docs PR. The buyer is a DevRel or docs team at a dev-tool company.

The business plan sets the agent's spending limit. `firstrun econ` reads every neatlogs trace, cfo.ai turns the costs into a per-tier cap, and `firstrun run --tier` stops any run that spends past it.

cfo.ai model, public and read-only: [https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE)

## Three Tiers Price by Quickstarts Covered

| Tier | Price per month | Quickstarts | Runs per month |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 1, weekly | 4 |
| Team | $49 | 10, nightly | 300 |
| Scale | $299 | 100, nightly, with PRs, Docs Bisect and Prerequisite Proof | 3,000 |

## The Average Run Costs $0.0167, but One in Twenty Costs Three Times That

neatlogs holds 64 `firstrun.run` traces from 2026-10-10. `firstrun econ` reads them and writes [`drivers.csv`](drivers.csv), the file cfo.ai imports. Each quantile row names the trace it came from, so a judge can open the trace behind any cost in the model.

| Driver | Cost per run | neatlogs trace |
|---|---|---|
| Mean | $0.01672 | all 64 |
| p50 | $0.01076 | `cef9cc00bcc5369d74ffc7fc5f525244` |
| p90 | $0.04424 | `ec246a27f83c9e11d682eb09a1818f58` |
| p95 | $0.05078 | `9e30cd0f9cee66410c81fb3a34e03177` |
| Max | $0.10135 | `a462576e751e91543b5623185331d603` |
| Compute | $0.0019 | assumption: AWS t3.medium at $0.0416 an hour for the measured 164.8 s mean |

The costs are Sonnet 5.5 list price, and Anthropic did not bill them. The 64 traces include 28 development runs, so the spread is wider than a production month would show.

The expensive runs are the useful ones. A run that hits a broken step pays for recovery and for the second clean run. Of 19 real-world runs, 10 ended `verified` with 32 proven patches, and the 19 runs cost $0.97 in total. That is $0.0975 per verified quickstart (source: `runs/*/state.json`).

## The Old $0.50 Cap Let a Scale Customer Cost Five Times the Price

Before this plan, every run had the same cap of $0.50 in `src/firstrun/models.py`. That cap was 30 times the mean run cost, and nothing in the business set it.

| Tier | Revenue per run | Margin at mean cost | Margin at p95 cost | Margin if every run hits $0.50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Team | $0.1633 | 88.6% | 67.7% | -207.3% |
| Scale | $0.0997 | 81.3% | 47.1% | -403.6% |

The mean says both tiers are healthy. The p95 says Scale falls below a 70% margin in a month with many broken quickstarts. The old cap says one bad month can cost a Scale customer's fee five times over.

## The Margin Floor Sets the Cap, and the Agent Enforces It

The founder picks one number, a 70% gross margin floor. The cap for each tier is the model spend one run may use and still keep that floor:

```text
cap per run = price / runs per month x (1 - margin floor) - compute per run
```

If every run in a month hits the cap, the tier still earns 70%. A Free run has no revenue, so its cap is the measured median run.

| Tier | Cap per run | Measured runs over the cap |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0.0108 | 48.4% |
| Team | $0.0471 | 7.8% |
| Scale | $0.0280 | 25.0% |

## The Planner Fix From the Traces Cut Cost per Run by 24%

neatlogs Detections and an Investigate run found the planner inventing steps. The fix shipped in commit 3ca6f11. The same 4 targets, before and after, as neatlogs measured them:

| Agent | Model cost per run | Quickstarts finished | Failed steps recovered |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | $0.0262 | 2 of 4 | 0 |
| v2 | $0.0200 | 3 of 4 | 3 |

## cfo.ai Shows the Old Cap Runs Out of Cash in Month 14

Ari built the model in cfo.ai over MCP, in workspace "Atharva CFOAI", page "FirstRun model". Every formula reads its number from a "FirstRun drivers" table, and its "Driver source" column names the neatlogs trace behind each measured cost. The figures below were read back from cfo.ai, not computed by hand. Cost per run is $0.01862, the 64-trace mean plus compute. Gross margin includes Stripe fees.
41:| 1:00 to 2:00 | Office hour with Chetan Raj, booked 2026-10-09. Bring a real trace, the title card and the README. | His answers saved in `hackathon.md` | Ask the 3 questions in Discord instead |

## Five Mentors, and the One Question for Each

**Booked: Chetan Raj (2026-10-09).** Use him for packaging, because he is a frontend architect who builds and tests consumer agents. Ask him three things:

1. "Where does a judge stop trusting a demo?" Show 30 seconds of a real run, from the terminal to the trace.
2. "FirstRun has no web UI. Is the terminal plus the report plus neatlogs enough, or does one static HTML report page make the result clearer?" Add the page only if he says yes and Layer 2 is done.
3. "Does the README sell it in 10 seconds?"

Bring a real trace, `META/Attachments/neathack/brand/title-card-1920x1080.jpg` and the README. Rohan Mukherjee was the first pick for the verification question. Ask him in Discord instead.

| Mentor | Who | Ask this in office hours | Links |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rohan Mukherjee | Proximal (RL environments and evals for coding agents, $15M seed). Ex-Dyte founding engineer, ex-Cloudflare AI Gateway. | "How do I stop FirstRun from gaming its own verification run?" | [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roerohan/) · [X](https://x.com/roerohan) |
| Ankush Dharkar | Founder of TrueHuman.id and Real Dev Squad. 28.8K X followers, the largest audience of the ten. | "What is the smallest human-in-the-loop check that makes an agent trustworthy?" Also: "What makes a dev audience share a build post?" | [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ankushdharkar/) · [X](https://x.com/ankushdharkar) |
| Rithvik K | ML engineer, Palantir SWE, research grantee at Adoption AI. | "How should state survive a crash halfway through a long run?" | [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rithvik1709/) · [X](https://x.com/BngRithvik) |
| Karan Pargal | Claims 16+ hackathon wins. Web3 and trading systems. His own profiles still say Covalent/Trench, not Confido Health. | "What do the first 30 seconds of a winning demo video show?" | [LinkedIn](https://in.linkedin.com/in/karan-pargal) · [X](https://x.com/karan_pargal) |

1	---
2	name: banger-tweets
3	description: Create engaging X (Twitter) posts that drive engagement and grow audience. Use this skill when asked to write X/Twitter content, craft viral tweets, or help with X engagement strategy. Triggers include requests for tweets, X posts, or social media content for X. Atharva is on X Premium+, so one post carries up to 25,000 characters and threads are retired.
4	---
5	
6	# Writing X Posts
7	
8	## Gate. Do these five things before you draft a single tweet
9	
10	This applies to every request, including a one-line lazy prompt like "tweets about this". A short prompt does not mean a short procedure.
11	
12	1. **Load the chain.** `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, then
13	   `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, then `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, then `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, then this file. Nothing else
14	   loads for a tweet. Render the load-order (the sequence rule files load in) panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill banger-tweets --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<the idea>"`. It looks the chain up itself and runs every scorer that applies, so the checks half is measured rather than typed. `--glob` takes a batch.
15	2. **Check for a matching Substack Note.** Run `python SCRIPTS/socials/parity.py --file "<the tweet
16	   file>"`. It pairs on `series` plus `sequence` first, then `source_blog`, then the title. When it
17	   names a Note, that Note is the material and the source article is not. Copy every number and
18	   claim across, then rewrite in the register below. See the parity rule in `SOCIALS/README.md`.
19	3. **Read `references/examples.md` in full.** It is not optional background. It is the calibration, and a draft written without it comes out as a summary instead of a tweet. If you skipped it, you are about to write the bad version. Part 1 holds real tweets from writers Atharva reads, each with the mechanic named, and it sets the bar. Part 2 holds the same shapes in his voice, and it sets the register. Read Part 1 first.
20	4. **Write the take for each tweet before you write the tweet.** One sentence, stating something Atharva believes and would defend. If you cannot state it, you do not have a tweet, you have a fact. Then name the take's box from `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. Only box 4 becomes a tweet: non-obvious and usable today.
21	   Then run the opening gate in `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md` on the first line. A tweet whose best fact sits in its last line moves that fact to the top.
22	5. **Never restate a banned word here.** The lists live in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` and reach you
23	   through `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. The shapes a regex cannot catch live in `core/pattern-rules.md`.
24	
25	Then output this table before any drafts. It is short on purpose and it exists so the work is visible and checkable.
26	
27	| # | Take (what he believes) | Box (net new value) | Shape | Evidence backing it |
28	|---|---|---|---|---|
29	
30	Never skip the table. It is the difference between drafting and reporting.
31	
32	## When a tweet will not start, borrow a winning shape
33	
34	[Swipefile](https://swipefile.com/) holds about 14,000 tagged examples that already worked, including 903 social and X posts, 3,214 copywriting entries and 2,433 advice entries. Each one carries a short teardown of why it worked. Use [swipefile.com/category/social](https://swipefile.com/category/social) for X specifically.
35	
36	Borrow the shape, never the words. The take stays Atharva's and the evidence stays his. A swiped hook with his claim under it is a tweet. A swiped hook with a swiped claim is theft and it reads like someone else.
37	
38	Read the full entry in `LIBRARY/Lists/tools and software directory.md`.
39	
40	## The one rule that fixes 90% of bad tweets
41	
42	**The claim leads. The evidence backs it up.**
43	
44	A tweet that opens by naming a company, a study, a person, or a report has already failed, because the subject of the sentence becomes "someone did research" instead of "here is what is true".
45	
46	Mechanical test, run it on every draft: **read only the first six words.** If those words name a source, rewrite so the first six words say what you believe.
47	
48	```
49	broken:  SparkToro measured their own accounts and found posts with links reach 10x fewer people.
50	fixed:   a post with a link reaches 10x fewer people than the same post without one. meta wrote
51	         that advice into their own help docs. they're not hiding the toll booth. you keep paying it.
52	```
53	
54	Same fact. The first is a press release. The second costs the reader something.
55	
56	When you are handed raw material (an article, a blog, a situation), find the sharpest uncomfortable truth inside it. That single sentence is the tweet. Everything else is packaging.
57	
58	> **Where the angle comes from.** Pick the subject and argument shape from `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Content Formats - 100 Post Ideas.md`, top 10 first. That file never chooses the wording. Everything below governs how the tweet reads, and a tweet that sounds like a LinkedIn post has failed no matter which format it came from.
59	
60	## No links in the post
61	
62	An X post carries no URL. Not to the blog, not to a repository, not to a tool. X cuts the reach of a post that sends the reader off the platform, and Atharva pays that toll on every scheduled post.
63	
64	This binds hardest on anything going out through Zernio, because those post on a schedule with nobody watching the numbers. Write the post so it stands alone and pays the reader on X.
65	
66	Three ways to keep the value without the link.
67	
68	**Name the thing.** "the glossary" and "pocketflow" cost nothing and a reader who wants it can search.
69	
70	**Give the substance away.** The post carries the number, the rule or the step. A reader who wants the rest goes looking without being told to.
71	
72	**End on the claim.** A post that ends on a URL taught the reader that the post was an advertisement. End on the sentence that was worth reading.
73	
74	Never replace a link with "link in bio", "link in the replies", or "DM me for it". Those are the same toll with extra steps.
75	
76	## One post, never a thread
77	
78	Atharva is on X Premium+. One post holds up to 25,000 characters, so the reason threads existed is gone. Three rules follow from that and none of them bends.
79	
80	**Never number a post.** No `1/`, no `2/`, no `🧵`, no "a thread". A point that needed three numbered parts is one post that runs longer.
81	
82	**Never write a pinned comment.** The pinned first comment is a LinkedIn mechanic and it belongs to `write-linkedin-posts` alone. On X the link goes in the post body.
83	
84	**Never split one argument across posts.** If part two only makes sense after part one, they are one post.
85	
86	A file may still hold several posts separated by `---`, and that is a batch of independent posts, never a sequence. Each one stands alone and the reader can meet them in any order. A post regenerated from a Substack Note is the exception: that file holds exactly one post, because the pairing is one to one.
87	
88	Length is a reach decision, not a rule. Short travels further, so stay short by default. Run long when the material is a system dump, or when the post carries its matching Note in full. Count the characters against 25,000 rather than estimating.
89	
90	## Shapes. Pick one per tweet, never blend, rotate across a set
91	
92	A set of 15 tweets that all use the same shape is one tweet written 15 times. Rotate deliberately. You cannot write a greentext about a study, which is the point: the shape forces different thinking.
93	
94	**One-liner / nuke.** One sentence, no context, complete on its own.
95	`your CI pipeline being green doesn't mean the code works`
96	
97	**Deadpan.** States something absurd like everyone already knows it. The flat delivery is the joke.
98	`running the same claude opus prompt 8 times because "maybe this time"`
99	
100	**Staircase.** Lines get shorter, weight falls on the last one. White space does the work.
101	```
102	1,000 google searches
103	415 produce a click
104	360 land on a site google doesn't own
105	
106	that's the open web's entire share
107	```
108	
109	**Reverse pyramid.** Wide, then narrow, then one line that implodes.
110	
111	**Greentext.** `>` lines, sequential, self-deprecating, ends `>mfw`. For things that went wrong. Write the arrow as a literal `>`, never as `>`, because the scorer reads the entity's semicolon as a banned semicolon and fails the file on one CRIT per line.
112	```
113	>read that video outperforms
114	>buy a camera
115	>learn premiere
116	>post to linkedin
117	>reaches 10x fewer people than plain text
118	>mfw
119	```
120	
121	**Fragment.** Trails off. Lets the reader finish it.
122	`prompt caching exists and you're just...`
123	
124	**Cocky take.** No hedging, no "in my experience". States it confidently. Invites the quote-tweet disagreement, which is free distribution.
125	`if your AI output sounds generic you gave it nothing. the model is fine. you are the problem.`
126	
127	**Dry flex.** An achievement stated so flatly the lack of celebration is the flex.
128	
129	**Shower thought.** Sounds offhand, cuts deep, makes people stop.
130	`"direct traffic" is your analytics tool saying "i don't know."`
131	
132	**Story beat.** One real specific moment. No lesson attached to the end.
133	
134	**Heuristic.** Name the trigger, name the correction, give the direction. The reader can run it tomorrow. Strongest shape in the mined corpus, so reach for it more than you think.
135	
136	**Field note.** One mundane place or moment used as a sensor for a large trend. Dated, specific, and it stops before the lesson.
137	
138	**Timestamped contrast.** Two dates, two lines, no commentary. `2008: build an app / 2023: build an app store`
139	
140	**Dialogue.** A short transcript where the contradiction accuses the subject for you. One calm line of commentary after, at most.
141	
142	**System dump.** The long post that lists a real working setup step by step. Every step names a tool and a trigger, every number is real, and it never closes on "comment X and I'll DM you". The shape most likely to run long, since X Premium+ now carries that length in the post itself.
143	
144	Match shape to energy: hurts because true → one-liner or shower thought. Embarrassing → greentext or story beat. Can't believe it works this way → deadpan or fragment. Stating it without apology → cocky take. The visual has to land → staircase or pyramid.
145	
146	## Voice
147	
148	Lowercase reads casual and confident. Fragments are fine when the meaning is clear. No hedging, no "in my experience", no "this is just me". Specificity beats generality every time, so write "4 years" and "$340", never "a long time" and "a lot". Dark humor is fair game and self-deprecation earns trust. Silence the editor that wants to explain the joke.
149	
150	## Hard bans
151	
152	**Hook shapes:** "Unpopular opinion:", "Hot take:", "Nobody talks about this", "I used to think X. I was wrong.", "Steal this", "[Year] taught me [lesson]", "Here's what I learned:", "A thread 🧵". Also never open on a question, per Voice.md.
153	
154	**Thread furniture:** `1/`, `2/`, `🧵`, "thread below", "more in the replies", and any pinned-comment line. All four are retired, see the one-post rule above.
155	
156	**Closers:** "What do you think?", "Drop your thoughts below", "Tag someone who needs this", "Follow me for more", "Retweet if you agree", "Save this".
157	
158	**Constructions:** the banned words, the negative parallelism forms and the tricolon cap are all in `slop_rules.py`, already in context. The copula dodge and the other shapes sit in section 1 of `core/pattern-rules.md`. Do not restate either list here, and do not treat the absence of a restatement as permission.
159	
160	**AI tells specific to X:** perfect symmetry between setup and payoff, every tweet ending on a lesson, a clean three-act structure inside one tweet, explaining the joke in the last line. None of these four is in the scorer, so they are checked by reading.
161	
162	## The judge pass. Score your own drafts before he sees them
163	
164	Run this after the drafts exist and before the six mechanical checks. Score every tweet out of 5 on each axis, print the table, and rewrite anything below 18. Judging your own work feels redundant and it is the step that catches the three failures a read-through never does.
165	
166	| Axis | 5 looks like | 1 looks like |
167	|---|---|---|
168	| Claim | He would defend this in a reply thread | A fact with no position on it |
169	| Specificity | Names, numbers, exact strings | "the best people", "a lot", "recently" |
170	| Register | Sounds like him out loud | Sounds like a caption |
171	| Standalone | Works with every other tweet covered | Needs the set to make sense |
172	| Shape fidelity | Matches the shape's real mechanic | Wears the shape's label only |
173	
174	Three failure modes score low every time, so hunt them by name.
175	
176	**The vague superlative.** "the four sharpest people i read", "one of the best threads", "a huge corpus". You have the names and the numbers in the material you were handed, so put them in. @nabeelqu's heuristic works because it quotes the exact sentence that triggers it. Any superlative without a name attached is an unfinished draft.
177	
178	**Rhythm beating accuracy.** A line that scans better than the truth. Merging two tools into one, rounding a cost up, saying "paid" about something free. Every factual claim traces back to something that actually happened, and the version that scans worse ships.
179	
180	**The borrowed line as payload.** Quoting someone else's sentence and letting it carry the tweet. The reader remembers them, not him. Quote someone only when your own take is the larger half, and never as the closing line.
181	
182	## Before you hand it over
183	
184	Run all nine. A failure on any one means rewrite, not ship.
185	
186	1. **First six words of every tweet.** Any that name a source get rewritten.
187	2. **Shape rotation.** No two consecutive tweets share a shape, and no set leans on one shape.
188	3. **Negative parallelism scan.** Search every draft for the word "not" and for "isn't". Any tweet built as `X. not Y.` or as `this is not X, it is Y` gets rewritten to say Y on its own. This is the single most common construction that survives a first draft, so scan for it by hand rather than trusting a read-through.
189	4. **Character count.** The ceiling is 25,000 characters, not 280, because Atharva is on X Premium+. Count characters, do not estimate. Most posts still stay short, because a short post reads better and travels further.
190	5. **Thread scan.** Search every draft for `1/`, for `🧵`, and for the word "thread". Any hit is a rewrite into one post. Search for "pinned" as well, because that mechanic belongs to LinkedIn.
191	   **Link scan.** Search for `http`. Any hit comes out, including a link to his own blog. Search for "link in" too.
192	6. **Standalone check.** Cover every other post in the file. Does this one still work alone?
193	7. **Scorer.** `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` and CRIT must reach 0. Ignore the flow, paragraph and fragment findings, which are long-form rules that do not apply to short-form.
194	
195	Run `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"` as well, and take CRIT to 0. It asks whether a reader outside this vault can follow the piece. Every CRIT names a term coined here, so searching the web gives the reader the wrong meaning and only a gloss on the page fixes it. A PostToolUse hook blocks the write while a CRIT stands.
196	8. **Pattern rules.** Section 7 of `core/pattern-rules.md`, run after the scorer. Then section 6 of the same file, because a set of tweets edited flat is worse than a set with one tell left in it.
197	9. **Uniqueness.** `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md`, five questions. A tweet that fails question 1 (his frame, not just the fact) or question 5 (would any other account post this) does not ship.
198	
199	## Output order
200	
201	Show the take table, then the drafts, then the judge table with the rewrites already applied. Hand him the scored set rather than a first pass, because a draft he has to grade himself is work you moved onto his desk.
202	
203	## Where the file goes
204	
205	Check for an existing placeholder before writing anything. One file per topic per channel, never duplicate, never write outside `SOCIALS/Tweets/`.
206	
207	Look for `SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_[Exact Blog Title].md`. If it exists, write into it. If it does not, create it.
208	
209	```markdown
210	---
211	type: Tweet
212	title: Exact Blog Title
213	source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
214	description: "The hook, one line"
215	created: YYYY-MM-DD
216	updated: YYYY-MM-DD
217	posted: false
218	---
219	
220	[the post, immediately, nothing between it and the frontmatter]
221	```
222	
223	A post regenerated from a Substack Note carries `series` and `sequence` copied from that Note, because those two fields are what pair the file to it.
224	
225	Use `source_blog: none` for original content with no source article. Never emit a `#tweet` tag and never emit a `**Source Blog:**` line, both retired 2026-07-27. Never put an extra `---` between the frontmatter and the post, because a stray one reads as a block break.
226	
227	One file usually holds one post. A batch file may hold several independent posts separated by `---` on its own line, and the review desk shows each as its own card. Never number them, because they are not a sequence. A file paired to a Note holds exactly one post.
228	
229	## Output
230	
231	Show the take table, then the tweets. Add one line on why a shape fits only where it is genuinely interesting. Skip emoji headers, skip a "WHY THIS WORKS" section, skip the recap.
232

8	
9	# Voice, Tone & Style Guide
10	
11	> **Purpose:** To ensure all generated content sounds unmistakably like Atharva. See [About](./About.md) for identity and [Principles](./Principles.md) for the underlying philosophy.
12	>
13	> **Above this file:** [AI Writing Policy](./AI%20Writing%20Policy.md) is the central directive. It outranks this guide and every rule in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`. Read it first.
14	>
15	> **Related:** [[AI Slop Is a Skill Issue -- Bad Inputs Made Bad Outputs Long Before AI|AI Slop Is a Skill Issue]] (the published manifesto on why inputs matter), [Audience](./Audience.md) (who we write for)
16	
17	## Tonal Attributes
18	
19	| Attribute      | Description                             | Example                                                                                   |
20	| :------------- | :-------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
21	| **Direct**     | No preamble. Cut straight to the value. | _"Stop optimizing your logo. Fix your H1 tag."_                                           |
22	| **Technical**  | Use precise engineering terminology.    | _"The latency bottleneck is in the edge worker, not the DB."_                             |
23	| **Analytical** | Skeptical of hype, reliant on numbers.  | _"The graph shows a 20% drop, despite the new UI."_                                       |
24	| **Witty**      | Occasional dry humor.                   | _"It works on my machine, which is the engineer's equivalent of 'thoughts and prayers'."_ |
25	| **Empathetic** | Understanding the pain of the builder.  | _"I know, configuring Webpack is hell. Here's a template."_                               |
26	
27	## The signature
28	
29	Tone attributes tell a model how to sound polite. This section is the part a reader recognises as
30	you, and it exists because 79 published articles opened in five different registers and none of them
31	matched. Added 2026-08-09, see item 17 in `SUBSTACK/TODO.md`. Correct it rather than trusting it,
32	because it was assembled from the vault and not from a conversation with you.
33	
34	**Stance.** Write from a position. The authority is quiet and comes from having done the work, so
35	state the conclusion plainly and let the evidence carry it. Never perform confidence, never posture,
36	never write to sound clever. The register is a well-read adult explaining something they understand
37	completely to another adult, which means no slang, no exclamation, and no straining for edge. You
38	should be able to take any subject, including one outside your field, and hand the reader a better
39	map than they arrived with. Where you are guessing, say so once and move on.
40	
41	**The reference layer.** This is the strongest voice signal you have and the most underused. You
42	think in film, books, games, and startups, so let the analogies come from there instead of from the
43	generic business shelf. A cinematography choice explains a product decision better than a sports
44	metaphor does. Two or three per article is a voice, and one per paragraph is a tic. The reference
45	has to do real explanatory work, because a name dropped for recognition alone is decoration and
46	reads as showing off. Assume the reader has not seen the film, so make the point land either way.
47	
48	**Openers make a claim.** The first sentence states something you believe and are about to defend.
49	It never asks the reader a question, never announces what the article will cover, and never
50	explains who the article is for. If the opener would survive being printed alone on a card, it
51	works.
52	
53	Wrong: "Ever felt like you're living in a dream, even when you're wide awake?"
54	Wrong: "I created this list to help anyone, especially Gen Z professionals and career-switchers."
55	Right: "Most startups do not die because they ran out of money. They die because they ran out of
56	attention."
57	
58	**The test.** Strip the byline and the topic from any two of your articles. A reader who knows your
59	work should still place them with the same author. If they cannot, the piece is written in the
60	voice of its subject rather than in yours.
61	
62	## Writing Style
63	
64	**Voice & grammar**
65	- Use active voice. Right: "Management canceled the meeting." Wrong: "The meeting was canceled."
66	- Address readers directly with "you" and "your."
67	- Be direct and concise. Simple language. No fluff.
68	- Simplify grammar where natural. Example: "yeah we can do that tomorrow."
69	
70	**Rhythm & flow**
71	- Vary sentence structures (short, medium, long) to create rhythm. Example: "Stop. Think about what happened. Consider how we might prevent similar issues in the future."
72	- Mix short punchy sentences with longer explanatory ones.
73	- Use simple punctuation that keeps readers moving forward.
74	- Maintain a natural, conversational tone.
75	
76	**Specificity & confidence**
77	- Use concrete, specific language. Right: "Let's meet to discuss how to improve this project." Wrong: "Let's touch base to move the needle on this mission-critical deliverable."
78	- Choose definitive statements over conditionals. Say "this works" not "this might work."
79	- Avoid marketing language. Right: "Our tool helps you track expenses." Wrong: "Our cutting-edge solution delivers unparalleled results."
80	
81	## Banned words, phrases, punctuation and style
82	
83	Defined in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` only, and nowhere else. Check a file with
84	`python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"`. Add a new ban to that file, never to this one.
85	
86	## Formatting rules, the Atharva style
87	
88	These are persona and formatting calls that a regex cannot make. The banned lists live in
89	`slop_rules.py`.
90	
91	1. Break large blocks of text into bullets or short paragraphs.
92	2. Bold the key insight so a skimmer catches the value. Outside `SUBSTACK/`, mid-sentence bold is fine. Inside `SUBSTACK/`, bold only a label that opens a line.
93	3. Give a code example where one applies.
94	4. Write a header as a conclusive statement. Wrong: "Where they actually break." Right: "The disagreement that matters."
95	5. Link every source and tool that you name.
96	6. Use no hyphen inside a compound word. Write "second brain", never "second-brain".
97	7. Use no hashtags and no emoji, unless I ask for one.
98	8. Say what a thing does. Never call it "powerful" or "best-in-class".
99	
100	## "Before & After" Examples
101	
102	**Before (Generic AI):**
103	"It is really important to optimize your website for SEO because it helps you get more traffic. There are many tools you can use like Semrush."
104	
105	**After (Atharva Digital Twin):**
106	"**SEO is a distribution channel, not a checkbox.** If your LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) is >2.5s, Google penalizes you. Don't guess; use **Semrush** or just check PageSpeed Insights. Fix the speed, then worry about the keywords."
107	
108	## How to edit my text
109	
110	1. Keep my ideas, claims, point of view, tense and structure. Change only what breaks a rule.
111	2. Keep the length close to the original.
112	3. Invent no fact, story, metric or promise.
113	4. Output the edited text only. Add no commentary.
114	5. Stay skeptical. Check a claim before you keep it, because accuracy beats polish.
115	6. Replace "In a world where" with the change and its result, stated directly.
116	7. Replace "Most people do X" with one specific observation or with my own tactic.
117	8. Replace "Stop X. Start Y." with the reason, the condition, or the steps.
118	9. Keep the response dense. Add an example when it earns its space.
119	10. Use an informative tone. State the fact without sugar-coating it.
120

8	
9	# Pattern Rules
10	
11	> **Purpose:** `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` catches words. This file catches shapes. A draft can
12	> score CRIT 0 and still read like a machine wrote it, because the tell is the sentence structure
13	> and not the vocabulary. Loaded on every writing job, right after the runtime contract.
14	>
15	> Sections 1 to 4 say what to remove. Section 5 says what to leave alone, and it carries the same
16	> weight. Adapted from `core/anti-ai-rules.md` and `core/ai_slop_commandments.md` in
17	> [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer). The mechanism notes are
18	> theirs. The wording and the thresholds are mine.
19	
20	Each rule below names the pattern, the mechanism that produces it, and the fix. The mechanism
21	matters. A rule you understand survives a rewrite, and a rule you memorised does not.
22	
23	## 1. Sentence shapes
24	
25	**The copula dodge.** A model replaces `is` with `serves as`, `stands as`, `represents`, `marks`,
26	`boasts`, `features` or `offers`. The mechanism is a repetition penalty. The model avoids reusing
27	the common word `is`, and the substitute implies a relationship that does not exist. Write `is`.
28	Keep `serves as` only where a real function sits beyond plain identity.
29	
30	**Tacked-on analysis.** A participle clause bolted to the end of a sentence to fake depth. The
31	shapes are `highlighting its importance`, `underscoring the shift`, `reflecting a broader trend`
32	and `marking a significant moment`. These clauses carry no new fact. They claim the fact before
33	them matters and supply no evidence. Cut the clause. If the significance is real, write it as its
34	own sentence with its own proof.
35	
36	**Unearned significance.** A claim of impact, legacy or scale with no support in the same
37	paragraph. Watch for `a pivotal moment`, `a key turning point`, `setting the stage for` and
38	`an enduring legacy`. Training data rewards important-sounding prose, so the
39	model asserts importance and expects the evidence to arrive later. State only what the evidence
40	carries. Real significance falls out of the evidence on its own.
41	
42	**The courtroom noun.** A judgment word standing in for a result nobody adjudicated. `verdict` is the
43	current one, and it arrives as `so the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation`
44	or as `the verdict is still out`. The same move hides in `ruling`, `the jury is out`, `case closed`,
45	`indictment` and `exonerates`. Two things break at once. The noun is a metaphor doing the work of a
46	number, and the `not a verdict, it's Y` frame negates a word the reader never proposed, which is the
47	banned antithesis with a straw man inside it. Write the result, the number, or the reason you cannot
48	tell yet. Keep the word where a real decision with named values exists, such as a court, or software
49	that emits one.
50	
51	**Vague authority.** A claim attributed to an unnamed group. `Experts agree`, `studies suggest`,
52	`research shows`, `observers note` and `industry reports indicate` all simulate a source. Name the
53	expert, link the study, or drop the claim. There is no third option.
54	
55	**The false range.** A `from X to Y` span where X and Y do not sit on one spectrum. The sentence
56	`From innovation to cultural change, AI is rewriting everything` reads as coverage and states
57	nothing. Name the two or three real things.
58	
59	**Name-dropping.** A list of outlets, tools or names with no fact attached. `Featured in Forbes,
60	TechCrunch and Wired` names sources and says nothing. The model lists authority to borrow it. Pick
61	one name and say what it said, or cut the list.
62	
63	**Abstract metaphor nouns.** A concrete idea dressed as a technical term. The set is `substrate`,
64	`vector` used for a way, `locus`, `vantage`, `nexus`, `bedrock`, `modality` and `endgame`. Each one
65	reads as precise and hides a plainer word: `base`, `way`, `place`, `last phase`. Pick the plain
66	word. His own working terms are exempt, because he chose them on purpose. `harness`, `flywheel`,
67	`scaffolding`, `surface` and `primitive` stay. The precedence ladder in the runtime contract
68	settles any other case, and it favours his voice.
69	
70	**The aphorism formula.** An ordinary claim dressed as reusable wisdom. The shapes are
71	`X is the currency of Y`, `the architecture of X` and `X becomes a trap`. This sounds
72	profound and loses the fact. Rule 23 in `slop_rules.py` bans the clever one-liner. This is the
73	same failure with a formula behind it, so replace the formula with the concrete claim under it.
74	
75	**The theatrical opener.** A standalone `Honestly?`, `Look,`, `Real talk` or `Here is the thing`
76	placed before an ordinary point. The tell is the fake reveal, because a person being honest just
77	says the thing. The same words mid-sentence in casual prose are ordinary English, so read the
78	position and not the word.
79	
80	**Adverbs propping up weak verbs.** `He ran very quickly` hides `he sprinted`. When the adverb is
81	load-bearing, the verb is wrong. Replace the verb and delete the adverb.
82	
83	**Elegant variation.** The model renames its subject to avoid repeating it, so one person becomes
84	`the researcher`, then `the prominent figure`, then `the key player`. Rule 28 says one word for one
85	thing. This is the mechanism it defends against. Repeat the real name.
86	
87	## 2. Paragraph and section shapes
88	
89	**False balance.** The three-step formula runs positive framing, then a nod at problems, then
90	instant dismissal. `Despite these challenges, the opportunity is enormous` is the shape of
91	analysis with none of the work. Engage the problem and let it stand, or drop the pretence.
92	
93	**Tricolon saturation.** The rule of three is a real device and a model reaches for it by default,
94	because three items look thorough with no need to be thorough. One tricolon per paragraph, never
95	two in a row. Four real items get listed as four. Two real items get written as prose.
96	
97	**The outline wrapper.** Section titles that a template chose rather than the content. The set is
98	`Challenges and future directions`, `Key takeaways`, `Legacy and impact`, `Overview` and
99	`Background`. Each one announces generation before a reader reads a word. Rule 4 in `Voice.md`
100	already demands a heading that states a conclusion, so name what the section delivers.
101	
102	**Fractal recapping.** A summary before a section starts, and another after it ends. Both
103	`In this section we will cover` and `as we have seen` are padding inherited from textbooks. Rule 15
104	bans the trailing summary, and this rule bans the leading one. Write forward.
105	
106	**Diff-anchored writing.** Prose that narrates a change instead of describing the thing. The line
107	`This section replaces the old onboarding flow` only makes sense to a reader who saw the old one. A
108	changelog, a release note and a migration guide are version-scoped by nature and are exempt.
109	Everything else reads coherently to a reader who arrived today.
110	
111	**One-point dilution.** The same claim restated ten times across four thousand words, sold as depth.
112	Say the claim once. Then spend the length on evidence, on the counterargument, and on what follows.
113	
114	**The undone claim.** A later line quietly reverses an earlier one. The hook promises a result and the
115	close hedges it. A post says "about thirty minutes" and its pinned comment says "under one hour". Each
116	line reads fine alone, so the writer is the least likely person to see it. Read line 1 against line 2,
117	line 2 against the body, the ending against the opening, and the pinned comment against the post. Fix
118	the weaker line and leave the stronger one. Never rewrite both.
119	
120	**The echo stack.** Three or more consecutive lines built on one skeleton, such as "The page lacks X.
121	There is no Y. Z does not exist." The model repeats the last structure it wrote, and a person
122	escalates. Make each line add a fact or raise the cost, keep the strongest, and put the rest in one
123	list whose items differ in shape. Swapping synonyms into the same skeleton keeps the echo.
124	
125	## 3. Fill that is not content
126	
127	**Assistant bleed.** The set is `I hope this helps`, `Certainly`, `Would you like me to`,
128	`Feel free to adjust` and `Here is a draft of`. Each one belongs in a chat window, and inside a
129	deliverable each one is contamination. Start with the content.
130	
131	**Cutoff disclaimers.** The set is `As of my last update`, `while specific details are limited`
132	and `based on available information`. Each one is a hedge formatted as content. Say the honest
133	thing once instead, or ask him.
134	
135	**Placeholder leakage.** An unfilled field that ships. `[insert link]`, `INSERT_SOURCE_URL`,
136	`access-date 2026-XX-XX` and `add image if available` all reach the reader when nobody re-read the
137	draft. A bracket from the fabrication rule is deliberate and stays visible on purpose. A bracket
138	from a template is a defect.
139	
140	**Promotional register.** The set is `nestled`, `in the heart of`, `vibrant`, `boasts`, `renowned`
141	and `a diverse array`. All of it comes from tourism copy and press releases. Write the neutral
142	declarative version instead.
143	Rule 8 in `Voice.md` says the same thing from the other side, so say what the thing does.
144	
145	## 4. Formatting tells
146	
147	**Em dash density.** Already CRIT in `slop_rules.py`, so this is the reason behind that ban. Model
148	output uses the em dash far above human rates and puts it where a comma belongs. Do not trade the em
149	dash for parentheses or an en dash. That move swaps one tell for another. End the sentence, or use a
150	comma.
151	
152	**The colon as a connector.** A colon that joins two clauses mid-sentence fakes a cause. The line
153	`The fix is simple: you rewrite the query` adds nothing that a period would not. A colon is correct
154	before a list or an example. Everywhere else, end the sentence. Rule 17 in `slop_rules.py` already
155	bans a colon in a heading, and this is the same tell inside a line.
156	
157	**Bold on every key phrase in running prose.** Emphasis stops meaning anything once it is
158	everywhere. Reserve bold for a term you are defining, or for a label that opens a line. Rule 2 in
159	`Voice.md` sets the boundary per folder. A bold label must earn its place with a new fact after it.
160	`**Performance:** Performance improved 40%` fails, because the label only repeats the line.
161	`**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file` passes, because the detail is new.
162	
163	**Sentence case in an H2.** Every H2 uses AP Title Case, in every channel, and states the claim
164	its section proves. `SCRIPTS/slop/heading_case.py` blocks a miscased H2 and flags a topic label.
165	H1 and H3 and below keep the case their destination uses. A model that capitalises every word of
166	an H3 or a body label is still showing the old tell.
167	
168	**A skipped heading level, or a rule above every heading.** Jumping H2 to H4, or dropping `---`
169	before each section by reflex, are both template tics. Neither is a writing choice.
170	
171	## 5. What to leave alone
172	
173	Sections 1 to 4 are a list of things to remove. Applied without judgement they produce the second
174	failure, which is prose stripped so hard that nobody is home. That output is not human. It is a
175	different machine's output, and it is the source of every complaint that edited writing reads flat,
176	boring and sanded down.
177	
178	**None of the following is evidence of AI on its own.** Do not cut one unless it sits in a cluster
179	with real tells.
180	
181	- Clean grammar and a consistent style. Many writers are edited. Polish proves nothing.
182	- Formal vocabulary. The banned list names specific overused words. It does not ban intelligence.
183	  Leave "ostensibly", "notwithstanding" and "constituent" where they are the right word.
184	- A mix of casual and formal register. That usually marks a technical writer, not a chatbot.
185	- Dry, plain prose. For a runbook it is correct.
186	- One transition word. A single "however" is English. The pile-up is the tell.
187	- One short emphatic sentence. People land points with a clipped sentence. Flag the drumbeat only
188	  when several stack up and inflate the tone.
189	- A salutation or a sign-off. Letters are older than chatbots.
190	- An unsourced claim. Most writing is unsourced. That is a rigor problem and not an AI problem.
191	- A watched word inside a quotation, a title, a proper noun or an example. When the piece discusses
192	  the phrase rather than uses it, leave it exactly as written.
193	
194	## 6. What to protect
195	
196	Removing tells is half the job. The other half is leaving alive whatever was already alive. These
197	are the hardest things for a model to produce and the easiest for an eager edit to erase.
198	
199	- **Odd, specific, hard-to-invent detail.** A real address. A strange quote. "The lawyer who worked
200	  upstairs from my dentist." Models round specifics off and people hoard them. Never generalise one
201	  of these to make a sentence flow.
202	- **Mixed feelings left unresolved.** "I think this is mostly right and it still bothers me." A
203	  model defaults to a clean take. Do not resolve the tension for him.
204	- **Dated references.** Slang, a meme, an in-joke anchored to one year and one subculture. Models
205	  lag by a year, so these are strong human signal.
206	- **A genuine aside or a self-correction.** A parenthesis where the writer interrupts himself.
207	  Machines rarely do that.
208	- **Uneven rhythm.** A nine-word sentence next to a forty-word one. Model output drifts toward one
209	  uniform mid-length cadence. The variance is the signal, so never regularise it.
210	- **An opinion he can defend.** If he can say why he chose a word, that reasoning outranks every
211	  rule in this file.
212	- **A deliberate quirk.** A writer who always opens lowercase, or never uses a semicolon, is doing
213	  something. Match it.
214	
215	**The operating principle is clusters, not instances.** One em dash means nothing. An em dash plus
216	a tricolon plus "vibrant tapestry" plus a "Challenges" heading is a confession.
217	
218	When you cannot tell whether something is his voice or a machine default, the precedence ladder in
219	the runtime contract decides it. Assume it is his, and leave it.
220	
221	**When a draft carries none of the signals in section 6, the problem is not that AI patterns
222	remain.** The problem is that nobody is home. Adding a specific, a stance and some unevenness beats
223	deleting one more banned word. The fabrication rule sets the limit on how a specific gets added.
224	It comes from him, never from invention.
225	
226	## 7. The pass before you hand it over
227	
228	Run this after the scorer reaches CRIT 0, because the scorer cannot see any of it.
229	
230	- [ ] Any "serves as" or "represents a" standing in for "is"?
231	- [ ] Any tacked-on participle claiming significance?
232	- [ ] Any impact claim with no evidence beside it?
233	- [ ] Any unnamed authority carrying a fact?
234	- [ ] Two tricolons in a row, or a tricolon that hides four real items?
235	- [ ] A template heading, a leading recap, or a trailing recap?
236	- [ ] Any assistant bleed, cutoff hedge or leftover placeholder?
237	- [ ] Any colon joining two clauses where a period belongs?
238	- [ ] Any bold label that only repeats the line after it?
239	- [ ] Any metaphor noun where a plain word fits, outside his working terms?
240	- [ ] Any list of names or outlets with no fact attached?
241	- [ ] Any fact, name, number or source that he did not supply?
242	- [ ] Does any later line undo an earlier one? Read the hook against line 2, the body against the pinned comment, and the ending against the opening.
243	- [ ] Cover everything after the opening. Can you still guess how the piece ends? If so, the hook answered itself.
244	- [ ] Did anything from section 5 get cut that should have stayed?
245	- [ ] Did every signal in section 6 survive the edit?
246	- [ ] List every heading in the draft on one line. Does any heading state an outline slot rather than a claim, so it would sit unchanged over a different topic?
247	- [ ] Find the one sentence in the draft that only Atharva could have written: a real date, a named person, a number from his own work, a moment he was wrong. If no such sentence exists, the draft is not done.
248	- [ ] If the piece covers several parallel items, read only the closing line of each one in a row. Do they all sound interchangeable with the nouns swapped?
249	
250	## 7b. Fixing a MED without creating the next one
251	
252	Each advisory the scorer raises has one right fix. The other fix costs four to six rounds of
253	edit-and-rescore, and that is where most of the time on a clean draft goes.
254	
255	**`readability-fragment` and `readability-bullet-fragment`: add a finite verb, never merge.**
256	"Speed multiplier." becomes "A speed multiplier finishes their own tasks faster." Do not fold
257	the fragment into the sentence before it. Measured across `2_PUBLISHED` and `1_DRAFTS` on
258	2026-08-29: adding a verb created a new `ste-long-sentence` hit in 0 of 239 paragraphs, and
259	merging created one in 6. A fragment caps at nine words and a long sentence starts at
260	twenty-one, so a verb cannot cross the gap. A merge can.
261	
262	**`repeated-consecutive-opener`: escalate, do not reword.** Three lines that open on the same word
263	are an echo stack (section 2). Keep the strongest line, make each other line add a fact or raise the
264	cost, or fold the weak ones into one list whose items differ in shape.
265	
266	**`ste-long-sentence`: split at the clause, and check the halves.** Halving a 45-word
267	sentence leaves two 22-word sentences, both still over. Cut to the real clause boundary
268	instead, or drop a subordinate clause outright.
269	
270	**`ste-progressive` and `ste-perfect`: change the tense, do not restructure.** "They were
271	publishing videos" becomes "They published videos". A rewrite around the verb pulls a
272	fragment or a long sentence in behind it.
273	
274	**`readability-long-paragraph`: cut a sentence, do not join two.** Joining two sentences to
275	lower the count is the move that produces a long sentence. The scorer now only raises this
276	when the paragraph still holds a sentence over 20 words, so splitting one is always safe.
277	
278	## 8. Corpus-level shapes
279	
280	Sections 1 to 4 catch a tell inside one sentence or one paragraph. These four hide at the
281	scale of the whole piece, or across many pieces, so a single-file read misses them. The 2026-08-28
282	audit of all 78 published articles found each one repeating across most of the corpus, on
283	unrelated topics, which is what told a reader the pattern was the machine and not the writer.
284	Full findings: [AI Slop Reader Audit, 2026-08-28](../../INBOX/Reports/AI-Slop-Reader-Audit-2026-08-28.md).
285	
286	**The generic macro-skeleton.** Hook, why-it-matters, a numbered list or a run of parallel
287	sections, a recap, a closing call to action. A reader who has read enough AI explainers
288	recognizes this shape before evaluating a single claim in it, because the same headings
289	("Why This Matters", "Key Takeaways", "The Bigger Takeaway", "Wrapping Up", "Who This Is For")
290	would sit unchanged over almost any other topic. A heading must name the specific claim inside
291	its section, not the outline slot it fills. Found in roughly 83% of the audited corpus.
292	
293	**Zero first-person specificity.** Strip the byline and the piece runs unchanged on any other
294	blog covering the same topic, because every example is a generic hypothetical "you" or an
295	unnamed archetype rather than a named person, a real date, a real number from his own work, or
296	a moment he was wrong or surprised. This is the concrete thing a "reads AI" complaint detects,
297	even when the reader cannot name a rule. Every piece needs at least one detail only Atharva
298	could supply, woven into the opening or the close, not bolted on as an afterthought paragraph.
299	Found in roughly 64% of the audited corpus, the single most common reason cited.
300	
301	**Per-item template stamping.** When a piece covers several parallel items (tools, films,
302	terms, chapters, entries in a series), every item runs through the identical clause-by-clause
303	mold: same heading shape, same bolded lead-in, same closing "lesson" sentence. A reader can
304	predict item 4 after reading item 2, which reads as one template with new nouns dropped in
305	rather than several separate acts of thinking. Vary structure across items on purpose: let
306	length, opening move, and closing move differ per entry so no two are interchangeable with the
307	nouns swapped. Concentrated in, but not limited to, multi-part series (Film School in Scenes,
308	Slaying Your 20s, the Uketsu deep dives) and long enumerations (a glossary, a tool roundup).
309	
310	**Announcing significance instead of demonstrating it.** Stock transition phrases that promise
311	weight the next sentence has not earned yet: "Here's the thing", "Here is what matters", "Let
312	me explain", "Here's the part most people miss". Stacking two or three of these in one short
313	piece reads as connective filler standing in for an actual transition. Delete the announcing
314	sentence and let the next sentence open the paragraph directly. If the paragraph reads weaker
315	without the announcement, the claim itself is not strong enough yet, so rewrite the claim
316	rather than propping it up with a preamble.
317	
318	A fifth shape from the same audit is not new prose to avoid, it is a gap in the mechanical
319	scorer: "X is not Y. It is Z." across two full sentences performs the exact negate-then-reveal
320	move that `ANTITHESIS_PATTERNS` in `slop_rules.py` already bans when it is joined by a comma,
321	and slips past untouched because the scorer checks one sentence at a time. Treat it as banned
322	under the same rule until the detector is extended to match across a sentence boundary.
323	
324	## 9. The Wikipedia cross-check, 2026-08-28
325	
326	Atharva ran [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing)
327	plus a companion 38-badge detector list against this file. Most of the 38 were already covered by
328	a rule above under different wording (not-only-but-also, it's-important-to-note, testament,
329	crucial role, the ever-evolving landscape, the challenges-and-outlook formula, the tacked-on
330	participle, promotional boilerplate, chatbot leftovers). The genuine gaps are now mechanically
331	enforced in `slop_rules.py` and `score.py` rather than restated here, see `TIC_PATTERNS`,
332	`HARD_PHRASES`, and the stacked-questions and echoing-sentences checks in `score.py` for the
333	mechanism and the exact strings. Do not copy that list into this file, it would drift.
334	
335	A second pass on the same day built a probe file with one example sentence per badge and ran the
336	scorer over it. That probe found 20 of the 38 still silent, so the first pass had missed more than
337	it claimed. The 20 landed as 9 new regex shapes in `TIC_PATTERNS`, 4 advisory shapes in the new
338	`TIC_PATTERNS_SOFT`, a `repeated-consecutive-opener` run check in `score.py`, and about 50 new
339	fixed strings in `HARD_PHRASES` and `SOFT_PHRASES`. A backtest over 607 files across the vault, the
340	website and the marketing repo fired the new CRIT rules 35 times in total, and every hit read as a
341	real tic. Four dev-blog strings ("sane defaults", "zero config", "zero-config", "batteries
342	included") were demoted to SOFT in that backtest, because Airflow `default_args` advice and a
343	release note for a cache store both used them literally and correctly.
344	
345	Two writer-facing gaps closed with them. `rules_prompt.py` never rendered the tics, so the gate
346	blocked shapes the generated block in `CLAUDE.md` never named, and the banned headings had the same
347	problem. Both now render, and `TIC_DESCRIPTIONS` in `slop_rules.py` carries the plain-English form
348	of every tic. `rules_prompt.py` exits with an error when a tic has no description, so a new regex
349	cannot ship invisible to the writer.
350	
351	One item was deliberately left out. The source list flags a colon opening onto three or more
352	items ("separate ports, processes, and local state") and says so itself: noisy in technical
353	writing, off by default for a documentation corpus. Section 4 already states the opposite case as
354	correct here ("A colon is correct before a list or an example"), and this vault's own prose uses
355	that construction constantly and on purpose. Banning it would fail correct writing, so it stays a
356	human judgement call, not a scorer rule.
357

8	
9	# Net New Value
10	
11	> **Purpose:** This file decides whether an idea is worth drafting at all. The other core files
12	> decide how the draft reads. It loads for every channel: LinkedIn, X, Substack Notes, Substack
13	> articles and anything else Atharva publishes. Adapted from a creator post Atharva saved on
14	> 2026-09-25. The two-by-two grid is theirs. The application to this vault is his.
15	
16	## Only Box 4 Ships, on Every Channel
17	
18	Every insight sits on two axes. Is it obvious to the reader, or new to them? Is it tactical, so
19	the reader can act on it today, or is it only an idea?
20	
21	| | Non-tactical | Tactical |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| **Obvious** | Box 1. The reader ignores it. | Box 2. The reader skims it, because it confirms what they believe. |
24	| **Non-obvious** | Box 3. The reader repeats it to a friend and does nothing. | **Box 4, Net New Value.** The reader saves it and uses it the same day. |
25	
26	Net New Value means box 4: an insight the reader has not heard, with a step they can take now.
27	
28	The source uses a sleep coach to show all four boxes. Box 1 is "get more rest". Box 2 is "sleep 8
29	hours a night". Box 3 is "you build up sleep debt even when you feel fine". Box 4 is the coffee nap.
30	The reader drinks a coffee, naps for 20 minutes, and wakes up as the caffeine takes effect.
31	
32	The same grid in Atharva's own field reads like this.
33	
34	1. Box 1. "Use AI carefully in your writing."
35	2. Box 2. "Put your writing rules in CLAUDE.md."
36	3. Box 3. "Most rules in a CLAUDE.md never reach the draft."
37	4. Box 4. "Put the rule in a PostToolUse hook, a script Claude Code runs after each file write.
38	   Let it run the scorer and return `decision: block`, so a draft with a CRIT cannot save." This is
39	   how `.claude/hooks/writing-gate.py` works.
40	
41	## Run the Test Before the First Line
42	
43	Write the insight as one sentence before you draft. Then answer three questions in writing.
44	
45	1. Which box is it in? Say the box number.
46	2. What does the reader do in the next two minutes because of this piece? Name the exact action.
47	3. Where have they already heard it? If the answer is "every other account in the niche", it is
48	   box 1 or box 2, however well it is phrased.
49	
50	A box 4 insight goes to the channel skill. Anything else gets one upgrade attempt, then it goes back
51	to the idea bank.
52	
53	## Upgrade the Box by Adding the Missing Axis
54	
55	A box below 4 lacks one axis or both. The fix is to add the axis that is missing.
56	
57	1. Box 3 has the surprise and lacks the step. Add the exact command, number, tool name or order of
58	   operations that turns the fact into an action.
59	2. Box 2 has the step and lacks the surprise. Find what Atharva's own build showed that the common
60	   advice gets wrong, and lead with that.
61	3. Box 1 lacks both. Cut it. Polish on a box 1 idea produces a well-written post that nobody saves.
62	
63	A long article can carry box 2 and box 3 material as setup. The headline claim and every section's
64	claim must still be box 4, or the article is a summary of the field.
65	
66	## New Packaging Counts, Invented Facts Do Not
67	
68	The source reports a client who gained 10,000 followers from one post. She learned nothing new for
69	it. She packaged what she already knew in a form her readers had never seen. So box 4 usually comes
70	from Atharva's own builds, numbers and mistakes, which no other account has.
71	
72	The fabrication rule in `core/runtime-contract.md` still holds. Never invent a number, a result or a
73	step to push an idea into box 4. When the tactical detail is missing, ask Atharva for it or mark the
74	gap as `[the real step]`.
